# The admin site

2024-04-28

In the previous section, we discussed how to design the database. The main issue with this is that anyone who wants to edit data would still need to know how to code. Most people in the world (and very likely your workplace) will not be technical, and they will also have a need to edit data in the backend.

Django provides an "admin" app by default to help your non-technical administrators change the database by themselves. We will set it up in this section.

## `createsuperuser`

Run this command to create a user account with administrator privileges. This type of account is typically called a "superuser" among software professionals.

```bash
python manage.py createsuperuser
```

You will be prompted for a username, an email, and a password. We will assume that you chose `cafeadmin` as your username.

Start the server and navigate to `http://localhost:8000/admin`. Here, you will be able to log in as the superuser you just created. Note, though, that your Product model from your `core` app will not be available. To make it available on the admin site, you will need to register the model in `core/admin.py`.

```python
from django.contrib import admin

from .models import Product

# Register your models here.

admin.site.register(Product)
```

1 # Users 2 3 2024-04-29 4 5 We now arrive at a large problem in developing web apps. Most web apps (as opposed to web sites) require some sort of interaction from users. Most web apps also need to track which specific users performed which specific actions. Some web apps need to prevent users from taking actions if they are not logged in. 6 7 Django's answer to the question of users is to provide a User model by default. Django's User model comes with an authentication framework, so you will not need to design one from scratch. The User model is also extensible: if you need to add additional fields to a User that aren't included by default, Django recommends that you create a model specific to your app and then join it one-to-one with the User model. 8 9 By default, the Django user authentication method is a "native login." This means that Django users usually login directly via a username and password. It has become very common for web apps to offer "federated login" through providers like Google and Facebook. While Django does support adding these login methods, for simplicity, we will not attempt to extend the native login in this walkthrough. 10 11 ## Protecting your existing pages 12 13 Let's do this backwards. The _first_ thing we will do is protect our two existing views, `index` and `product_detail`, against users who are not logged in. 14 15 Import the `login_requred` decorator from `django.contrib.auth.decorators`. A "decorator" is something that you add to the top of a function to modify its behavior. We will not be creating decorators in this walkthrough, but we will be using them. 16 17 ```python 18 from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required 19 ``` 20 21 Then, on top of both of your views, add the decorator. 22 23 ```python 24 @login_required 25 def index(request): 26 ... 27 28 @login_required 29 def product_detail(request, product_id): 30 ... 31 ``` 32 33 Try to reload the page. You should expect there to be an error. If you are not getting an error, try logging out of the admin site, which you may be logged into. Once you see an error, you may proceed. 34 35 ## The login view 36 37 It naturally follows that your `core` app needs to be able to log users in. This is usually done by creating a view specifically for login. By default, Django's `login_required` decorator tries to redirect unauthenticated users to `accounts/login`, but you can customize this by changing `settings.LOGIN_URL` or by providing a `login_url` keyword argument to the decorator. We will leave this as is for now. 38 39 Django does provide built-in views specifically for authentication, but for the purposes of this walkthrough, we will create our own view. Create a new function in `core/views.py` called `login_view`. Do not call it `login` to avoid naming conflicts with functions we will import later. 40 41 ```python 42 def login_view(request): 43 ... 44 ``` 45 46 This is where we will introduce an important concept in web apps: forms. A "form" is an HTML element that allows users to send input to the server. Let's create our form now in the `login_view` view. Create a new file `core/templates/core/login_view.html` and add this HTML code. 47 48 ```html 49

Login

50 {% if messages %} 51
    52 {% for message in messages %} 53 {{ message }} 54 {% endfor %} 55
56 {% endif %} 57
58 {% csrf_token %} 59 60 61 62 63 64
65 ``` 66 67 Note that this form has two new elements. 68 69 - The `{% if messages %}` block fetches what are usually called "flash" messages from Django. Flash messages are pieces of information that you might want to display to a user if some event (such as a failed login) occurs. You will see how this is used later. 70 - The `{% csrf_token %}` line here is a security feature that protects your route. It adds a secret, hidden field to the form that defends against the case where someone sends a POST request to your endpoint without actually trying to login. 71 72 Change the login view to render this new template. 73 74 ```python 75 def login_view(request): 76 template = loader.get_template("core/login_view.html") 77 context = {} 78 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 79 ``` 80 81 Register the login view with `core/urls.py`. 82 83 ```python 84 # Unfortunately, in this case, the trailing slash is REQUIRED. 85 path("accounts/login/", views.login_view, name="login_view"), 86 ``` 87 88 Now, when you try to visit any page while you are not logged in, you should get redirected to a login form. 89 90 Of course, our login form doesn't actually do anything right now. All it does when we press "Login" is send an HTTP POST request (as opposed to a normal HTTP GET request) to the `accounts/login/` route on our Django server. (The form's "method" property tells is to send a POST request, and the form's "action" property tells it to send to the same URL as the current URL.) We will need to modify our view to handle different types of requests. 91 92 Pause to consider the different types of requests that might hit `accounts/login/`. First, there is the normal GET request that comes when a user simply visits the site on their browser. In this case, we simply want to render the login HTML page. Second, there is the POST request that comes when a user fills out the login form and presses "Login." In this case, we want to check if their credentials are correct. If they are, we want to tell the Django server to log the user in, and we also want to redirect them to a page. 93 94 Import these new Django functions in `core/views.py`. 95 96 ```python 97 from django.shortcuts import redirect 98 from django.contrib.auth import ( 99 login, logout, authenticate 100 ) 101 from django.contrib import messages 102 ``` 103 104 Then, implement different codepaths for whether your view got a GET request or a POST request. 105 106 ```python 107 def login_view(request): 108 if request.method == 'GET': 109 template = loader.get_template("core/login_view.html") 110 context = {} 111 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 112 elif request.method == 'POST': 113 submitted_username = request.POST['username'] 114 submitted_password = request.POST['password'] 115 user_object = authenticate( 116 username=submitted_username, 117 password=submitted_password 118 ) 119 if user_object is None: 120 messages.add_message(request, messages.INFO, 'Invalid login.') 121 return redirect(request.path_info) 122 login(request, user_object) 123 return redirect('index') 124 ``` 125 126 Note a few things here. 127 128 - If the request was a POST request, you can access the key-value pairs submitted with the POST request in the `request.POST` object. In this case, since the POST request is sent by a form, the key-value pairs in the `reuqest.POST` object will correspond to the form fields. That is why we can expect a `username` and `password` key: the form itself had fields named `username` and `password`. 129 - The `authenticate` method here is supposed to return a User object if the login is successful and `None` if the login failed. If there is no User object, we want to simply redirect the user back to the login page. 130 - If the login failed, we also use the `messages` function to load a new message to be displayed in the flash messages upon the page redirect. Try failing a login intentionally to see this in action. 131 - The last line of the function, `return redirect('index')`, tells Django to redirect to the view named `index`. You can see in `core/urls.py` that we named one of our paths `index`. That is the view we want to redirect to. 132 133 You can now try to log into your site using the superuser you created in a previous section. Since users are shared between the admin site and the main site, this should work. If you don't remember your admin credentials, you can run `python manage.py createsuperuser` to try again. You can also manage users directly via the admin site. 134 135 Once you have implemented login, you can use the user that is currently logged in in your views. Try to change the index view to greet the user by username. You can get the current user from the request object like so. 136 137 ```python 138 @login_required 139 def index(request): 140 # Load the template 141 template = loader.get_template("core/index.html") 142 products = Product.objects.all() 143 context = { 144 "user": request.user, 145 "product_data": products, 146 } 147 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 148 ``` 149 150 Then, add this line somewhere at the top of `core/templates/core/index.html`. 151 152 ```html 153

Hi, {{ user.username }}!

154 ``` 155 156 ## Checkpoint 157 158 Take two screenshots: 159 160 - First, a screenshot of a failed login. 161 - Second, a screenshot of the new index page, greeting your user by username. 162

1 # The cart 2 3 2024-04-29 4 5 This is where all our Django experience now comes together. In this section, we will add the ability for users to add products to their cart. This feature will require us to touch almost every part of Django so far, from views to templates to models to routing. However, the hope is that it is crystal clear how Django helps you implement the feature. 6 7 ## Start with the model 8 9 Django becomes easier if you think of _everything_ as subordinate to the model. We should thus start here. 10 11 We only have two models right now: Product, which we made ourselves, and User, which we got out-of-the-box from Django. Pause to consider how you would model a shopping cart. Since this is a walkthrough, we will prescribe the model ourselves, but you should begin practicing data modeling now. 12 13 There will be one new model: CartItem. Each row of CartItem will represent one "line item" in the cart. A "line item" is a common concept in retail: it is composed of a product ID and a quantity. Together, many line items might make up a single transaction or, in this case, a single cart. 14 15 ```python 16 ... 17 from django.contrib.auth.models import User 18 ... 19 class CartItem(models.Model): 20 user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, null=False) 21 product = models.ForeignKey(Product, on_delete=models.CASCADE, null=False) 22 quantity = models.IntegerField() 23 def __str__(self): 24 return f'{self.quantity} of {self.product} (User: {self.user.username})' 25 ``` 26 27 For now, we will assume that each User only has one Cart, but that the Cart may contain many CartItems. If you have taken a basic data modeling class, you should understand this intuitively. If you haven't taken a basic data modeling class, try [this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xsg9BDiwiJE) video. 28 29 A CartItem is very much related to both the User who put the items in their cart and the Product that the user put into their cart. A CartItem should thus have _references_ to these other two tables. This is what _foreign keys_ are for. 30 31 We will now register our model. # Hello Django

2024-04-28

In this section of the Digital Cafe walkthrough, we will set up your Django project.

The rest of this walkthrough assumes that you are familiar with your terminal or are at least capable of learning it. We will also be using UNIX file path conventions: directories and files will be separated by forward slashes (e.g., `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/manage.py`). Mac OS follows UNIX file path conventions. If you are on Windows, forward slashes are replaced by backward slashes (e.g., `digitalcaferoot\digitalcafe\manage.py`).

## Django development approach

The original version of Digital Cafe was written using Flask, which is a Python web microframework. This version of Digital Cafe is written using Django, which is a much heavier framework.

If you come across the Flask version of Digital Cafe, you may notice that it is structured as many quick iterations. This was only possible (and desirable) because Flask is not opinionated about how to handle web app development. In the Django version of Digital Cafe, we need to take things a little more slowly and thoroughly. In a similar, inverted way, this is only possible and desirable because Django already has the answers for building web apps.

For example, the Flask version of Digital Cafe starts by storing the database in a dictionary before iterating to MongoDB. We do not do this in Django because we only have one option for our database: a relational database. Yes, there are different flavors of relational database (SQLite vs. PostgreSQL, for instance), but the choice is made for us to use a relational database.

Being railroaded like this has its benefits. It makes it less mentally taxing to build features if you know that there's only one real way to do it.

## Structure of a Django project

A Django project is composed of multiple layers of directories, which each have multiple files.

The directory you created in the previous section, `digitalcaferoot`, is what we will call the "true root" of the entire Django project. It is the umbrella directory that contains every other file related to your Django project. Your true root will contain your Python virtual environment, and it is where you will start your Django editing sessions.

We will now create a Django project. Run this command in your terminal window. Make sure your virtual environment is active.

```bash
django-admin startproject digitalcafe
```

This will create a new directory called `digitalcafe`. We will call this directory the "project root."

You should now see this file structure, starting from the project root:

```
digitalcafe
├── digitalcafe
│   ├── asgi.py
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── wsgi.py
└── manage.py
```

The top-level `digitalcafe` directory is the project root. The second-level `digitalcafe` is a _separate_ directory that we will call the "package directory." It contains more management files.

Let us briefly recap:

- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot` that is the "true root" of your entire Django project. It contains your Python virtual environment. When starting a coding session, you will usually start here and activate your virtual environment.
- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/` that is the "project root" of your Django project. It was created when you ran `django-admin startproject digitalcafe`. You will spend most of your terminal time here because it hosts `manage.py`, which is the file Django uses for command-line tasks.
- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/digitalcafe/` that is the "package directory" of your Django project.

Yes, it's confusing.

Thankfully, that's all we need to do to start your very first Django project. Navigate into the project root (i.e., `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/`) and run this command:

```bash
python manage.py runserver
```

Your terminal should display messages that it is now running a Django development server.

Open your web browser and navigate to the URL `http://localhost:8000`. This URL points to your local server; it can't be accessed by anyone else. You should now see a welcome page for Django, saying "The install worked successfully! Congratulations!"

## Checkpoint

Please take a screenshot of your browser, pointed at `http://localhost:8000`.

You can serve HTML as a file, or you can also serve it as a string from a web framework like Django. 6 7 ## Creating your webpage 8 9 There is a little more Django boilerplate we have to work through. # Project: Digital Cafe (Vibecoded)

This project recreates "Digital Cafe" — a Django + SQLite web app used to
teach ITMGT students web development. The original hand-built walkthrough
and spec live at: https://github.com/Alteheit/digitalcafe-2024
(see `doc/walkthrough/` in that repo, numbered from 0001 onward).

This time, the app is being rebuilt using an agentic coding workflow instead
of writing code by hand. You (the AI) will write all code. The human will
not write code directly — only give instructions, review your output, and
approve merges.

## Required Workflow

For every feature or change, follow this exact five-step process, in order.
Do not skip a step or combine steps unless explicitly told to.

1. **study** — Analyze the requested feature or change. Write a Markdown
   file in `doc/study/` discussing feasibility, tradeoffs, relevant parts
   of the existing codebase, and open questions. Do not write code yet.
   Name the file descriptively, e.g. `doc/study/0001-user-auth.md`.

2. **plan** — Based on the study, write a checklist Markdown file in
   `doc/plan/` with concrete, ordered, checkable steps needed to implement
   the feature. Name it to match the study, e.g. `doc/plan/0001-user-auth.md`.

3. **execute plan** — Create a new git branch off `main` for this feature
   (e.g. `feat/user-auth`). Execute the plan's steps on that branch,
   checking items off as you go. Make commits as you complete logical
   chunks of the plan, not just one giant commit at the end.

4. **rendezvous** — Once the plan is fully executed and the app is in a
   working state, merge the feature branch back into `main`. Before
   merging, verify the app actually runs and the feature works. Resolve
   any conflicts. Do not leave `main` in a broken state.

5. **sync docs** — After merging, update the living documentation in
   `doc/wiki/` so it accurately reflects the current state of the
   codebase (models, routes, features, setup instructions, etc.).
   Treat `doc/wiki/` as a manual for the codebase, not a changelog.

Never jump straight to writing code without a study and plan doc for that
feature first, unless the human explicitly says to skip ahead for a trivial
fix (e.g. a typo or one-line bug fix).

## Commit Conventions

All commits must use Conventional Commits format:
- `feat:` — a new feature
- `fix:` — a bug fix
- `chore:` — maintenance, config, tooling
- `build:` — build system or dependency changes
- `docs:` — documentation-only changes (including doc/study, doc/plan, doc/wiki)
- `refactor:` — code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
- `test:` — adding or fixing tests

Keep commit messages scoped to a single logical change.

## Folder Reference

- `doc/study/` — feasibility/tradeoff analysis docs, one per feature
- `doc/plan/` — checklist implementation docs, one per feature
- `doc/wiki/` — living manual of the current codebase (kept in sync after every rendezvous)

## Tech Stack

Django + SQLite, matching the original Digital Cafe (v2024). Do not
substitute a different framework or database without discussing it in a
study doc first.

## Notes for the Agent

- Reference the original walkthrough at

# Study: Digital Cafe MVP (products, cart, checkout, auth, admin, order history)

2026-09-12

## Goal

Build the full first version of Digital Cafe: a Django + SQLite app where a
logged-in user can browse products, add them to a cart, check out (turning
the cart into a transaction), view their past orders, and where a superuser
can manage all data through the Django admin.

This is a single large study covering the whole MVP rather than one study
per page, because the pieces (models, cart, checkout, order history) are
tightly coupled and were originally built as one continuous walkthrough.

## Reference material

Cloned `https://github.com/Alteheit/digitalcafe-2024` to a scratch directory
and read `doc/walkthrough/0001` through `0010`. Relevant takeaways:

- The original project layout is `digitalcaferoot/` (true root, holds the
  venv) `> digitalcafe/` (project root, holds `manage.py`) `>
  digitalcafe/` (package dir) and `core/` (the single app). This triple
  nesting exists because the walkthrough has students create the venv
  directory by hand before running `django-admin startproject`.
- A single app, `core`, holds everything: models, views, templates, urls.
- Views are plain functions (no class-based views, no DRF, no frontend
  framework), branching on `request.method`.
- `Product.price` is a plain `IntegerField` (whole pesos, no cents).
- Auth is native Django `django.contrib.auth`: a hand-rolled `login_view`
  using `authenticate()` / `login()` / `messages`, protected views via
  `@login_required`.
- `CartItem` links `User` + `Product` + `quantity`. The walkthrough does
  **not** merge duplicate `CartItem` rows for the same product — adding the
  same product twice just creates two rows.
- Checkout converts every `CartItem` for the current user into a
  `Transaction` + one `LineItem` per cart item, then deletes the `CartItem`
  rows. `Transaction.created_at` is set manually via
  `dt.datetime.now(tz=dt.timezone.utc)`.
- Order history ("transaction history") is explicitly left as an exercise
  in walkthrough 0010 — there is no reference implementation to copy for
  that page.

## Target repo layout

This repo (`digital-cafe-vibecoded/`) is already the git root and already
contains `CLAUDE.md` and `doc/`. There's no pedagogical reason to reproduce
the walkthrough's confusing triple-nested folder structure here, since a
human isn't being taught to run `django-admin startproject` by hand.

**Decision:** put the Django project directly at the repo root:

```
digital-cafe-vibecoded/
├── CLAUDE.md
├── doc/
├── manage.py
├── digitalcafe/        # package dir (settings, root urls, wsgi/asgi)
├── core/                # the one app: models, views, templates, urls, admin
├── requirements.txt
├── .gitignore
└── .venv/               # gitignored
```

This keeps the tech stack identical (Django + SQLite, per CLAUDE.md) while
dropping only the incidental folder-nesting choice, which the CLAUDE.md
tech-stack note doesn't mandate.

## Data models (`core/models.py`)

| Model | Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Product` | `name: CharField(max_length=100)`, `price: PositiveIntegerField` | Whole-currency-unit price, matching the original's `IntegerField` but non-negative. `__str__` returns `name`. |
| `CartItem` | `user: FK(User, CASCADE)`, `product: FK(Product, CASCADE)`, `quantity: PositiveIntegerField` | One row per (user, product) — see merging decision below. |
| `Transaction` | `user: FK(User, CASCADE)`, `created_at: DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | "timestamp" from the spec. `auto_now_add` instead of the walkthrough's manual `dt.datetime.now()` call — same result, less code, can't be forgotten. |
| `LineItem` | `transaction: FK(Transaction, CASCADE)`, `product: FK(Product, CASCADE)`, `quantity: PositiveIntegerField` | Snapshot of what was bought; deliberately does **not** snapshot price (see Open Questions). |

All FKs use `on_delete=models.CASCADE`, matching the walkthrough.

### Design decision: merge duplicate cart items

The spec says "CartItem: linked to a user and a product, with a quantity" —
singular, implying at most one `CartItem` per (user, product) pair, unlike
the walkthrough which allows duplicates. Merging is a small addition
(`get_or_create` + increment) and produces a materially better checkout
page (no duplicate product rows to visually add up). **Decision: enforce
one CartItem per (user, product) by incrementing quantity on repeat
add-to-cart**, enforced with a `unique_together`/`UniqueConstraint` on
`(user, product)`.

## Pages / views (`core/views.py`, `core/urls.py`)

| Path | View | Auth | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `index` | `@login_required` | Lists all products (name, price, link to detail). Greets user by first name if set, else username. |
| `/product/<int:product_id>/` | `product_detail` | `@login_required` | GET: shows name, price, add-to-cart form (quantity input). POST: upserts a `CartItem`, flash message, redirect to `index`. |
| `/accounts/login/` | Django's built-in `LoginView` w/ custom template | public | GET: login form. POST: on failure, Django's `AuthenticationForm` attaches a non-field error ("Please enter a correct username and password...") rendered in the template — satisfies "error message shown on failed login" without hand-rolling `authenticate()`/`messages` like the walkthrough did. |
| `/accounts/logout/` | Django's built-in `LogoutView` | `@login_required`-equivalent (POST) | Not in the original spec, but a login-gated app needs a way to log out to be usable/testable at all; minimal addition, uses Django's built-in view (no new code beyond a URL + settings). |
| `/checkout/` | `checkout` | `@login_required` | GET: shows current user's `CartItem`s with a "Checkout" button. POST: wraps cart in a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s, deletes the `CartItem`s, flash message, redirect to `index`. |
| `/orders/` | `order_history` | `@login_required` | New page (not in walkthrough). Lists the user's `Transaction`s newest-first, each with its `LineItem`s (product name, quantity). |
| `/admin/` | Django admin | superuser | Register `Product`, `CartItem`, `Transaction`, `LineItem`. |

### Why built-in `LoginView`/`LogoutView` instead of hand-rolled

CLAUDE.md's tech stack line calls for "Django's built-in
`django.contrib.auth` for username/password login" — the built-in
class-based auth views are literally part of that. They also give the
required failed-login error message for free and are less code to maintain
than the walkthrough's manual `authenticate()`/`messages` dance. All other
views stay function-based, matching the walkthrough's explicit preference
against class-based views ("We advise you to ignore this feature").

### Templates

A shared `core/templates/core/base.html` with a nav bar (Home / Checkout /
Order History / logout form) and a `{% if messages %}` block, extended by
`index.html`, `product_detail.html`, `checkout.html`, `order_history.html`.
`registration/login.html` for the login form (Django's default template
lookup path for `LoginView`). This avoids repeating the messages/nav
boilerplate on every page — a plain `{% extends %}` base template, not a
custom abstraction.

## Settings

- `INSTALLED_APPS` += `"core"`.
- `LOGIN_URL = "login"`, `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = "index"`, `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = "login"`.
- `DATABASES` stays the Django default `sqlite3` backend pointing at
  `db.sqlite3` in the repo root.
- `db.sqlite3` is gitignored (local/dev artifact, regenerated by
  `migrate`); a data migration seeds three sample products (Americano,
  Cappuccino, Espresso — same names/prices used as examples throughout the
  walkthrough) so the app is immediately exercisable after a fresh
  `migrate` without requiring manual admin data entry first.

## Testing

Add a small `core/tests.py` (Django `TestCase`) covering the parts most
likely to regress silently:
- anonymous access to `/`, `/product/<id>/`, `/checkout/`, `/orders/`
  redirects to login;
- add-to-cart creates a `CartItem`, and adding the same product twice
  merges quantity instead of duplicating the row;
- checkout converts cart to a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s and empties the
  cart;
- order history only shows the logged-in user's own transactions, not
  other users'.

This also gives a concrete, repeatable way to satisfy the rendezvous step's
"verify the app actually runs and the feature works" requirement, beyond
manually clicking through the dev server.

## Open questions

- **Price precision.** Spec just says "price," no currency/decimal
  requirement. Following the walkthrough's `IntegerField` convention
  (whole units, e.g. pesos) rather than introducing `DecimalField` and
  cents-handling that wasn't asked for. If real currency precision is
  needed later, that's a follow-up study.
- **Historical price on `LineItem`.** Right now `LineItem` has no `price`
  field, so if a `Product`'s price changes after a purchase, order history
  will display the *current* price, not the price paid. The spec's field
  list for `LineItem` (transaction, product, quantity) doesn't include
  price, so this matches spec as given, but it's a real gap for a
  production app. Flagging rather than silently adding an unrequested
  field.
- **Registration / sign-up page.** Not in the feature list. Assuming
  accounts are provisioned by the superuser via `/admin/` only (matches
  the walkthrough, which never builds a public registration page).
- **Removing/editing individual cart items on the checkout page.** Spec
  only asks for "showing the current cart contents" and a checkout button.
  Not adding per-item quantity edit/remove controls on that page since
  they weren't requested; users can still manage cart contents via repeat
  add-to-cart visits (which now merge quantity) or ask an admin.

## Risks / tradeoffs

- Putting `manage.py` at the repo root instead of nesting it (see layout
  decision above) is a deliberate, documented deviation from the
  walkthrough's exact folder shape — flagging here per CLAUDE.md's
  "discuss in a study doc first" rule for anything touching the prescribed
  tech stack, even though the framework/database themselves (Django +
  SQLite) are unchanged.
- Seeding sample products via a data migration is a small amount of extra
  code for convenience; if unwanted, it's trivially reversible (delete the
  migration, add products via admin instead).

human isn't being taught to run `django-admin startproject` by hand.

**Decision:** put the Django project directly at the repo root:

```
digital-cafe-vibecoded/
├── CLAUDE.md
├── doc/
├── manage.py
├── digitalcafe/        # package dir (settings, root urls, wsgi/asgi)
├── core/                # the one app: models, views, templates, urls, admin
├── requirements.txt
├── .gitignore
└── .venv/               # gitignored
```

This keeps the tech stack identical (Django + SQLite, per CLAUDE.md) while
dropping only the incidental folder-nesting choice, which the CLAUDE.md
tech-stack note doesn't mandate.

## Data models (`core/models.py`)

| Model | Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Product` | `name: CharField(max_length=100)`, `price: PositiveIntegerField` | Whole-currency-unit price, matching the original's `IntegerField` but non-negative. `__str__` returns `name`. |
| `CartItem` | `user: FK(User, CASCADE)`, `product: FK(Product, CASCADE)`, `quantity: PositiveIntegerField` | One row per (user, product) — see merging decision below. |
| `Transaction` | `user: FK(User, CASCADE)`, `created_at: DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)` | "timestamp" from the spec. `auto_now_add` instead of the walkthrough's manual `dt.datetime.now()` call — same result, less code, can't be forgotten. |
| `LineItem` | `transaction: FK(Transaction, CASCADE)`, `product: FK(Product, CASCADE)`, `quantity: PositiveIntegerField` | Snapshot of what was bought; deliberately does **not** snapshot price (see Open Questions). |

All FKs use `on_delete=models.CASCADE`, matching the walkthrough.

### Design decision: merge duplicate cart items

The spec says "CartItem: linked to a user and a product, with a quantity" —
singular, implying at most one `CartItem` per (user, product) pair, unlike
the walkthrough which allows duplicates. Merging is a small addition
(`get_or_create` + increment) and produces a materially better checkout
page (no duplicate product rows to visually add up). **Decision: enforce
one CartItem per (user, product) by incrementing quantity on repeat
add-to-cart**, enforced with a `unique_together`/`UniqueConstraint` on
`(user, product)`.

## Pages / views (`core/views.py`, `core/urls.py`)

| Path | View | Auth | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `index` | `@login_required` | Lists all products (name, price, link to detail). Greets user by first name if set, else username. |
| `/product/<int:product_id>/` | `product_detail` | `@login_required` | GET: shows name, price, add-to-cart form (quantity input). POST: upserts a `CartItem`, flash message, redirect to `index`. |
| `/accounts/login/` | Django's built-in `LoginView` w/ custom template | public | GET: login form. POST: on failure, Django's `AuthenticationForm` attaches a non-field error ("Please enter a correct username and password...") rendered in the template — satisfies "error message shown on failed login" without hand-rolling `authenticate()`/`messages` like the walkthrough did. |
| `/accounts/logout/` | Django's built-in `LogoutView` | `@login_required`-equivalent (POST) | Not in the original spec, but a login-gated app needs a way to log out to be usable/testable at all; minimal addition, uses Django's built-in view (no new code beyond a URL + settings). |
| `/checkout/` | `checkout` | `@login_required` | GET: shows current user's `CartItem`s with a "Checkout" button. POST: wraps cart in a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s, deletes the `CartItem`s, flash message, redirect to `index`. |
| `/orders/` | `order_history` | `@login_required` | New page (not in walkthrough). Lists the user's `Transaction`s newest-first, each with its `LineItem`s (product name, quantity). |
| `/admin/` | Django admin | superuser | Register `Product`, `CartItem`, `Transaction`, `LineItem`. |

### Why built-in `LoginView`/`LogoutView` instead of hand-rolled

CLAUDE.md's tech stack line calls for "Django's built-in
`django.contrib.auth` for username/password login" — the built-in
class-based auth views are literally part of that. They also give the
required failed-login error message for free and are less code to maintain
than the walkthrough's manual `authenticate()`/`messages` dance. All other
views stay function-based, matching the walkthrough's explicit preference
against class-based views ("We advise you to ignore this feature").

### Templates

A shared `core/templates/core/base.html` with a nav bar (Home / Checkout /
Order History / logout form) and a `{% if messages %}` block, extended by
`index.html`, `product_detail.html`, `checkout.html`, `order_history.html`.
`registration/login.html` for the login form (Django's default template
lookup path for `LoginView`). This avoids repeating the messages/nav
boilerplate on every page — a plain `{% extends %}` base template, not a
custom abstraction.

## Settings

- `INSTALLED_APPS` += `"core"`.
- `LOGIN_URL = "login"`, `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = "index"`, `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = "login"`.
- `DATABASES` stays the Django default `sqlite3` backend pointing at
  `db.sqlite3` in the repo root.
- `db.sqlite3` is gitignored (local/dev artifact, regenerated by
  `migrate`); a data migration seeds three sample products (Americano,
  Cappuccino, Espresso — same names/prices used as examples throughout the
  walkthrough) so the app is immediately exercisable after a fresh
  `migrate` without requiring manual admin data entry first.

## Testing

Add a small `core/tests.py` (Django `TestCase`) covering the parts most
likely to regress silently:
- anonymous access to `/`, `/product/<id>/`, `/checkout/`, `/orders/`
  redirects to login;
- add-to-cart creates a `CartItem`, and adding the same product twice
  merges quantity instead of duplicating the row;
- checkout converts cart to a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s and empties the
  cart;
- order history only shows the logged-in user's own transactions, not
  other users'.

This also gives a concrete, repeatable way to satisfy the rendezvous step's
"verify the app actually runs and the feature works" requirement, beyond
manually clicking through the dev server.

## Open questions

- **Price precision.** Spec just says "price," no currency/decimal
  requirement. Following the walkthrough's `IntegerField` convention
  (whole units, e.g. pesos) rather than introducing `DecimalField` and
  cents-handling that wasn't asked for. If real currency precision is
  needed later, that's a follow-up study.
- **Historical price on `LineItem`.** Right now `LineItem` has no `price`
  field, so if a `Product`'s price changes after a purchase, order history
  will display the *current* price, not the price paid. The spec's field
  list for `LineItem` (transaction, product, quantity) doesn't include
  price, so this matches spec as given, but it's a real gap for a
  production app. Flagging rather than silently adding an unrequested
  field.
- **Registration / sign-up page.** Not in the feature list. Assuming
  accounts are provisioned by the superuser via `/admin/` only (matches
  the walkthrough, which never builds a public registration page).
- **Removing/editing individual cart items on the checkout page.** Spec
  only asks for "showing the current cart contents" and a checkout button.
  Not adding per-item quantity edit/remove controls on that page since
  they weren't requested; users can still manage cart contents via repeat
  add-to-cart visits (which now merge quantity) or ask an admin.

## Risks / tradeoffs

- Putting `manage.py` at the repo root instead of nesting it (see layout
  decision above) is a deliberate, documented deviation from the
  walkthrough's exact folder shape — flagging here per CLAUDE.md's
  "discuss in a study doc first" rule for anything touching the prescribed
  tech stack, even though the framework/database themselves (Django +
  SQLite) are unchanged.
- Seeding sample products via a data migration is a small amount of extra
  code for convenience; if unwanted, it's trivially reversible (delete the
  migration, add products via admin instead).

from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse

from .models import CartItem, LineItem, Product, Transaction


class AnonymousAccessTests(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.product = Product.objects.create(name="Americano", price=110)

    def assert_redirects_to_login(self, url):
        response = self.client.get(url)
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 302)
        self.assertTrue(response.url.startswith(reverse("login")))

    def test_index_requires_login(self):
        self.assert_redirects_to_login(reverse("index"))

    def test_product_detail_requires_login(self):
        self.assert_redirects_to_login(reverse("product_detail", args=[self.product.id]))

    def test_checkout_requires_login(self):
        self.assert_redirects_to_login(reverse("checkout"))

    def test_order_history_requires_login(self):
        self.assert_redirects_to_login(reverse("order_history"))


class CartTests(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")
        self.product = Product.objects.create(name="Americano", price=110)
        self.client.login(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")

    def test_add_to_cart_creates_cart_item(self):
        self.client.post(reverse("product_detail", args=[self.product.id]), {"quantity": "2"})
        cart_item = CartItem.objects.get(user=self.user, product=self.product)
        self.assertEqual(cart_item.quantity, 2)

    def test_adding_same_product_twice_merges_quantity(self):
        url = reverse("product_detail", args=[self.product.id])
        self.client.post(url, {"quantity": "2"})
        self.client.post(url, {"quantity": "3"})
        self.assertEqual(CartItem.objects.filter(user=self.user, product=self.product).count(), 1)
        cart_item = CartItem.objects.get(user=self.user, product=self.product)
        self.assertEqual(cart_item.quantity, 5)

    def test_invalid_quantity_is_rejected(self):
        url = reverse("product_detail", args=[self.product.id])
        self.client.post(url, {"quantity": "0"})
        self.assertFalse(CartItem.objects.filter(user=self.user, product=self.product).exists())


class CheckoutTests(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")
        self.product = Product.objects.create(name="Americano", price=110)
        self.client.login(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")
        CartItem.objects.create(user=self.user, product=self.product, quantity=2)

    def test_checkout_converts_cart_to_transaction(self):
        self.client.post(reverse("checkout"))
        self.assertEqual(CartItem.objects.filter(user=self.user).count(), 0)
        transaction = Transaction.objects.get(user=self.user)
        line_items = LineItem.objects.filter(transaction=transaction)
        self.assertEqual(line_items.count(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(line_items.first().product, self.product)
        self.assertEqual(line_items.first().quantity, 2)

    def test_checkout_with_empty_cart_creates_no_transaction(self):
        CartItem.objects.filter(user=self.user).delete()
        self.client.post(reverse("checkout"))
        self.assertEqual(Transaction.objects.filter(user=self.user).count(), 0)


class OrderHistoryTests(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = User.objects.create_user(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")
        self.other_user = User.objects.create_user(username="bob", password="bob-pass-123")
        self.product = Product.objects.create(name="Americano", price=110)

        own_transaction = Transaction.objects.create(user=self.user)
        LineItem.objects.create(transaction=own_transaction, product=self.product, quantity=1)

        other_transaction = Transaction.objects.create(user=self.other_user)
        LineItem.objects.create(transaction=other_transaction, product=self.product, quantity=5)

    def test_order_history_only_shows_own_transactions(self):
        self.client.login(username="alice", password="alice-pass-123")
        response = self.client.get(reverse("order_history"))
        transactions = list(response.context["transactions"])
        self.assertEqual(len(transactions), 1)
        self.assertEqual(transactions[0].user, self.user)

# Setup and running the app

## Requirements

- Python 3.11
- A virtual environment (`.venv/` at the repo root, gitignored)

## First-time setup

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py createsuperuser
```

`migrate` also runs a data migration that seeds three sample products
(Americano, Cappuccino, Espresso) so the app has something to browse
immediately, without needing to add products via the admin first.

## Running the dev server

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python manage.py runserver
```

Visit `http://localhost:8000/`. You'll be redirected to
`http://localhost:8000/accounts/login/` until you log in with the
superuser (or any user) created above.

## Running tests

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python manage.py test core
```

Covers: login-gating of all protected pages, cart add/merge behavior,
checkout's cart→transaction conversion, and per-user scoping of order
history.

## Database

SQLite, file `db.sqlite3` at the repo root. It is gitignored — every
developer/environment runs their own `migrate` to create it locally. There
is no committed seed data beyond what the `core.0002_seed_sample_products`
migration inserts.

## Notable settings (`digitalcafe/settings.py`)

- `INSTALLED_APPS` includes `core`.
- `LOGIN_URL = "login"`, `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = "index"`,
  `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = "login"`.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["localhost", "127.0.0.1"]` (dev-only; would need
  updating for any real deployment).
- `DEBUG = True` (dev-only).

# Pages and routes

All application routes are function-based views in `core/views.py`,
wired in `core/urls.py` (included from `digitalcafe/urls.py` at the root
path). Every page except login requires an authenticated session
(`@login_required`); anonymous visitors are redirected to
`/accounts/login/?next=<original path>`.

| Path | Name | View | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `index` | `index` | Home page. Lists every `Product` (name, price), each linking to its detail page. Greets the user by first name (falls back to username). |
| `/product/<int:product_id>/` | `product_detail` | `product_detail` | GET: shows the product's name and price, plus an "add to cart" form (quantity input). POST: adds/merges the given quantity into the user's `CartItem` for that product, flashes a confirmation message, redirects to `/`. Non-positive or non-numeric quantity is rejected with a flash error and no cart change. |
| `/checkout/` | `checkout` | `checkout` | GET: shows the user's current cart contents in a table. POST: converts every `CartItem` into a `Transaction` + one `LineItem` each (atomically), deletes the `CartItem`s, flashes "Thank you for your purchase!", redirects to `/`. POSTing with an empty cart flashes an error and creates nothing. |
| `/orders/` | `order_history` | `order_history` | Lists the current user's `Transaction`s, newest first, each with its `LineItem`s (product name + quantity). Scoped strictly to `request.user` — other users' orders are never visible. |
| `/accounts/login/` | `login` | Django's built-in `LoginView` | GET: login form (`registration/login.html`). POST: on failure, shows "Please enter a correct username and password..." via the form's non-field errors. On success, redirects to `/` (`LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL`). |
| `/accounts/logout/` | `logout` | Django's built-in `LogoutView` | POST-only (per Django 5.x). Logs the user out and redirects to the login page. Triggered from the "Log out" button in the nav bar (a small form, not a link, because `LogoutView` no longer accepts GET). |
| `/admin/` | — | Django admin | Superuser-only. See [admin.md](admin.md). |

## Templates

- `core/templates/core/base.html` — shared layout: nav bar
  (Home / Checkout / Order History / logout, shown only when
  authenticated; a "Log in" link otherwise) and the `{% if messages %}`
  flash-message block. All other templates `{% extends %}` this one.
- `core/templates/core/index.html`, `product_detail.html`,
  `checkout.html`, `order_history.html` — one per page above.
- `core/templates/registration/login.html` — Django's default template
  lookup path for `LoginView`; not under `core/templates/core/`.

## Flash messages

Uses `django.contrib.messages`. Currently used for: add-to-cart
confirmation/validation errors, checkout success/empty-cart error, and
login failures (via the auth form's own error rendering, not the messages
framework).

# Admin site

Django's built-in admin app, mounted at `/admin/`. Access requires a
superuser account (`python manage.py createsuperuser`).

## Registered models (`core/admin.py`)

All four `core` models are registered with default `ModelAdmin` settings
(no custom list displays, filters, or search yet):

- `Product`
- `CartItem`
- `Transaction`
- `LineItem`

A superuser can create, view, edit, and delete rows of any of these
directly through the admin UI. This is currently the **only** way to add
new users or products — there is no public sign-up page or a
product-management page outside the admin (matches the original
walkthrough's scope; see `doc/study/0001-digital-cafe-mvp.md`).

## Managing users

The `User` model comes from `django.contrib.auth` and is also visible in
the admin (under "Authentication and Authorization"). Since the app has no
self-service registration, provisioning a new shopper account means either
`python manage.py createsuperuser` (for another admin) or creating a
regular `User` via the admin's "Users" section (for a shopper — leave
"Staff status" and "Superuser status" unchecked).
